title: Generalized Adaptive Boosting and the Geometry of Mistakes
claim: Boostability reduces to a geometric condition: a set of guarantees is boostable exactly when its convex hull avoids the trivial region.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, same axes, progressively more general cases
description: Four side-by-side 2-D plots share the same axes: false-positive guarantee z1 horizontally and false-negative guarantee z2 vertically. In each, a gray region labeled C with a curved boundary fills the upper right and represents trivial coin-attainable guarantees. A light-blue region marks the achievable guarantee set Z. Panel 1 has a linear triangular region below the line z1+z2 = 1/2-γ. Panel 2 has a single point with a rectangular down-closure. Panel 3 has several points, with a convex polygonal hull of the blue region staying clear of the gray. Panel 4 has two blue points on the axes joined by a dotted line, and a red star marks where that line touches the gray region. The eye goes first to the gray curved regions and the blue shapes.
caption: A visual depiction of our dichotomy theorem. In each plot, the two axes show the false-positive error guarantee $z_1$ and the false negative error guarantee $z_2$. The gray region is the set of "trivial" (coin-attainable) guarantees $\C$ (see [ref]). The blue region is (the down-closure of) some set of $(\FP,\FN)$ error guarantees $Z \subseteq [0,1]^2$ . In the left plot $Z=\{\bz\in[0,1]^2:z_1+z_2 \le 0.5-\gamma\}$, which is boostable by classic results. In the second plot $Z=\{\bz\}$ with $\bz \in [0,1]^2 \setminus \C$, which is boostable by the results of [ref]. In the third plot $Z$ is any subset of $[0,1]^2$ with $\conv(\overline{Z})\cap \C = \emptyset$; [ref] says this condition characterizes the boostable sets, therefore subsuming the two previous cases. In the rightmost plot, $Z=\{(0,\nicefrac{1}{2}),(\nicefrac{1}{2},0)\}$; while the two marked points are individually boostable, the set $Z$ is not as its convex hull touches $\C$.
abstract: Not all mistakes are alike. For example, in medical diagnosis, false positive and false negative mistakes have a different impact and should not be aggregated. By revisiting the classical theory of boosting through this lens, we introduce the notion of $Z$-learner, which returns weak hypotheses achieving joint false-positive/false-negative guarantees $(\mathrm{FP},\mathrm{FN})$ from some set $Z \subseteq [0,1]^2$. This formulation generalizes the standard notion of $Î³$-weak learning--recovered by taking $Z=\{(z_1,z_2): z_1+z_2<1/2-Î³\}$--and allows for more flexible notions of weak learnability that account for the impact of the distribution on the achievable learning guarantees. This raises a natural question: which sets $Z$ are boostable? We answer this by giving a complete geometric characterization that unifies, as special cases, both the classical boosting dichotomy and the recent multi-objective extension of Bressan et al. (COLT 2025). We also present an adaptive algorithm for boosting $Z$-learners without relying on the prior knowledge of $Z$, generalizing AdaBoost's ability to handle unknown margin parameters. Finally, we demonstrate that $Z$-learners can achieve confidence amplification. However, the analysis is significantly more involved than in classical boosting and relies on the centerpoint theorem from discrete and computational geometry.
